description: Very large (1.5 inch body) mature female Araneus orbweaver, most likely diadematus (garden cross). This specimen was found due to its extremely large geometric web (photograph 2), that was probably 3-4 feet in height, which was attached to the corner of the roof of a sunroom down to some hostas plants in a flower bed down below. A notable feature of the web, and interesting behavior of the spider, is it seems to have gathered two leaves to form a cubby or hideout at the bottom of the web (photograph 3-5) and when I first noticed the web the spider was not on it and was instead hiding inside the leaf cubby. I discovered this by lightly flicking the web, out of curiosity for who had made it, and watching as the giant female crawled out of hiding and into the center of the web, where I was able to collect photos. I theorize this leaf hide might serve multiple potential services. I believe it may be a combination of shelter from wind, protection from predators, and hiding from prey. On a windy day it makes more sense to chill inside here instead of blowing around on the web, which might have difficulties holding together due to her weight. Also due to her size, she may be easily spotted by predators such as birds, and might be using the leaves to hide. Lastly, I believe her size would also make her more visible to potential prey items who otherwise wouldn’t even notice the web, so she may be lying in disguise within the leaves until a prey item gets caught in her web.

Levi mentions *A. miniatus* having a pair of white longitudinal lines between the epigynum and spinnerets which I don't see here.  The scape on this spider seems long enough to rule out *A. partitus* in any case.

Still having trouble capturing fine details such as the wrinkles on the scape. Still working on making passable photos with my bargain bin equipment.  I will be trying to make some better epigyne photos with different lighting/magnification shortly.  I believe this is a mated female BTW.

description: Collected.

Earlier this week I identified this spider and found out it was the first reported listing of it in Fillmore County, MN. I also named it "Linda" because why not?

I speculate that Linda and her children are both completely nocturnal. They have a corner a bit from my window that they crawl back to every morning around 745am central. I also usually notice Linda and her babies coming out around 4-5 pm in the afternoon. I suspect this is purely an evolutionary hunting trait.

On the topic of hunting, tonight I got to witness Linda wrapping up a moth in her web! I almost felt proud for her. Soon after she was done though, she went to one of the younglings and started thrashing around. As did the youngling.

This thrashing started to look more like dancing, maybe celebrating a good hunt? I doubt it. But soon after that it became aggressive and confrontational. Both Linda and her child were raising they're legs up at each other in a territorial fashion. Linda then began striking at the younger spider. Once the younger spider backed off, Linda went back to her dancing.
